newsitem.title: USA: Alaska oil revenues above expectations.
newsitem.headline: Alaska oil revenues above expectations.

text.p: Higher-than-expected oil prices over recent months are expected to give Alaska a budget surplus for this fiscal year, erasing the $400 million shortfall forecast a year ago, state officials said on Friday.
The short-term spring forecast projected revenues of $2.45 billion for fiscal 1997, $30 million over the amount expected last fall, the Alaska Department of Revenue said.

The spring forecast pegs average prices of $20.80 a barrel for Alaska North Slope crude oil for the current fiscal year, which ends June 30. It forecasts prices of $18.44 for fiscal 1998 and $18.34 for fiscal 1999, the department said.

"We continue to see a growing global economy and strong crude oil demand," Wilson Condon, commissioner of the Alaska Department of Revenue, said in a statement. "While oil prices continue to exceed our expectations, we still forecast them to decline to historic levels."
The state's fiscal 1997 budget is expected to show a surplus of $15 million, said Bob King, spokesman for Gov. Tony Knowles.

Last year, when the Alaska legislature passed the state's fiscal 1997 budget, they believed the state would need to dip into a savings account over the year to fill an expected shortfall of about $400 million.
The Department of Revenue's report released Friday also forecast North Slope production would decline by 2.2 percent in fiscal 1998 and 3.9 percent in fiscal 1999.
However, oil production is expected to rebound in fiscal 2000 as Arco Alaska Inc.'s Alpine field and BP Exploration (Alaska) Inc.'s Northstar and Badami fields come on line, Condon said.
The department has estimated that those and other satellite fields will pump an additional $100 million into state coffers in fiscal 2002, increasing to $225 million in fiscal 2005, Condon said.
